title: 12 — Effective Field Theory and the Shape of Realism
paragraphs: Abdullah Afzal and Hassaan Saleem
Introduction

Modern physics presents us with a world that is hierarchical and structured in ways such that different physical regimes exhibit different dominant patterns. These patterns can often be captured by theories that are astonishingly accurate within their domains even while failing outside them. The resulting picture is one in which theories need not be fundamental in order to be true, and where understanding a physical phenomenon does not require knowing the details of arbitrarily short-distance physics. Instead, the behaviour of systems at accessible energies is frequently governed by structural principles, e.g., symmetries, conservation laws, and universality of some behaviours.

This layered structure of Nature is not a philosophical gloss but an empirical discovery. Nuclear reactions, atomic physics, condensed matter systems, gravitational interactions, and the early universe each exhibits patterns that can be described by theories effectively independent of the deeper dynamics that ultimately produce them. This insight, articulated with increasing clarity over the past halfcentury, has transformed not only particle physics and cosmology but also the philosophical interpretation of physical theories. The development of effective field theory (EFT) has made explicit what earlier physicists often sensed tacitly: that predictively successful theories need not aspire to fundamental status, but they succeed because they describe the emergent structures that dominate at particular scales, and those structures are robust under changes in microscopic detail.

This perspective also reframes familiar episodes in physics, such as the emergence of Fermi’s theory of beta decay, the optical explanation of why the sky is blue, and the modern understanding of general relativity not as stories of incorrect theories supplanted by truer ones, but as examples of how Nature simplifies when viewed at the right scale. We will shortly discuss these three examples in detail. Fermi’s four-particle interaction, though ultimately incomplete, captured the entire phenomenology of nuclear beta decay because the W boson is heavy. Rayleigh’s scattering law, derived long before the quantum structure of matter was understood, works because visible light is extremely long-wavelength compared to atomic scales. Moreover, general relativity, though incompatible with quantum field-theoretic methods, can be consistently treated as an EFT whose low-energy predictions are insensitive to the details of quantum gravity in the ultraviolet (a theory of quantum gravity that would hold true at very high energy scales). In each case, the simplicity and universality of the low-energy world arise from the fact that the physics at low energies becomes insensitive to the details of the physics at high energies.

These developments also bear directly on long-standing philosophical debates about scientific realism. The traditional realist view, according to which a scientific theory aims to describe the fundamental ontology of the world, sits uneasily with the scale-dependent structure revealed by modern physics. Quantum field theories require artificially introduced energy bounds to get rid of infinite quantities at low and high energies (these energy bounds are called regulators and cutoffs, respectively) that explicitly encode their non-fundamental character, and even classical theories like Newtonian mechanics derive their success from being the leading approximations to deeper relativistic dynamics. A rigid version of scientific realism threatens to declare nearly every successful theory we possess as false or incomplete in ways that undermine their ontological significance. However, this conclusion follows only if one assumes that realism of a theory must be tied to the “fundamentalness” of said theory.

The concept of effective realism offers a more compelling alternative. It begins with the recognition that what makes a theory realistworthy is not whether it achieves all-scale exactness but whether it captures the robust structures that remain invariant under changes of formulation, cutoff, and coarse-graining. This shift in emphasis aligns far more closely with scientific practice, where low-energy predictions are often insensitive to microscopic details, and where theories are routinely interpreted relationally, structurally, and within restricted domains. Effective realism becomes especially powerful when paired with ontic structural realism (OSR), which treats modal structure (meaning the pattern of what is possible, what is impossible, and what follows from what) and real patterns (instead of objects with intrinsic properties) as the primary ontological commitments. OSR provides the metaphysical grounding for why effective theories can be genuinely realist without being fundamental by stating that the structures they capture are real at their scale, and their robustness across derivations and models reflects the modal structure of the world.

Taken together, the EFT framework and the structural realist perspective also provide an understanding of the relationship between Newtonian and relativistic physics. The common narrative that special and general relativity “refuted” Newtonian mechanics obscures the deeper fact that Newtonian physics emerges naturally as the low-velocity, weak-field limit of the relativistic description. Far from being falsified, Newtonian mechanics identifies modal patterns like conservation laws, inertial structure, and gravitational potentials that remain real within the regime where they dominate. Relativity does not replace Newtonian physics, but it embeds it within a broader structural hierarchy, and this is precisely what effective realism and OSR would predict.

This article offers a brief account of these ideas. We begin with a careful exposition of effective field theories using Fermi’s theory of beta decay, Rayleigh scattering, and Donoghue’s work on treating general relativity as an EFT to illustrate how the logic of scale separation works in practice. We then turn to effective realism and its motivations within contemporary philosophy of physics, emphasising how EFTs reshape the landscape of realist commitments. Finally, we apply this conceptual framework to the relationship between Newtonian and relativistic physics, showing that the apparent replacement of Newtonian gravity by general relativity is better understood as a story of nested effective descriptions. Throughout, our goal is not merely to summarise technical developments but to highlight the unified picture of scientific explanation that emerges when effectiveness, scale separation, and structural realism are treated as central—not peripheral—features of physical theory.
Effective Field Theories

The idea of an effective theory is among the most powerful conceptual tools in modern physics, yet it remains widely misunderstood outside technical circles. It is often assumed that a theory in physics aims to be fundamental, an exact, all-scale description of the world. In this picture, when a new theory arrives, it replaces its predecessor the way a corrected equation replaces an incorrect one. But effective theories do not fit this narrative. They are not approximations in the sense of being imperfect guesses at the fundamental laws. Instead, they are precise, systematically organised descriptions of the macroscopic manifestations of deeper physics. Their predictive success does not depend on knowing the details of physics at high energies. The physics at high energies is dictated by phenomena at short distances (that is why high-energy physics is also called short-distance physics), and this physics can be very different from the everyday physics we see. For example, particles can behave as waves at the atomic scales, but we do not see wave-like behaviour of objects in our everyday life. Physical theories exploit the remarkable fact that physics at low energies becomes insensitive to physics at very high energies. This separation of scales is not an accident but a structural feature of the world.

An effective field theory (EFT) is a mathematical framework that expresses this idea in its most refined form. It is more than a truncated model. An EFT tells you exactly which features of the shortdistance theory matter for long-distance predictions and which are irrelevant. It organises ignorance and knowledge in a principled way, allowing one to calculate observable quantities to any desired level of precision without committing to a detailed theory of the very small length scales. The crucial point is that at any fixed precision, only finitely many parameters matter. The effects of everything else are typically proportional to the powers of the ratio between the energy you probe and the much higher cutoff scale. This effect is often referred to by saying that these effects are suppressed by the cutoff.

The idea of EFTs is strongly tied to the idea of Renormalisation group (RG) flows, which is the systematic way that physicists describe what changes and what stays the same as you zoom from short distances to long distances. Consider an EFT (called T₁) with an energy cutoff Λ₁. If we take a coarse-grained version of this EFT by keeping all the degrees of freedom with energies below another cutoff Λ₂ (where Λ₂ < Λ₁) and integrating over all the degrees of freedom with energies E such that Λ₂ ≤ E < Λ₁, then we get another EFT with cutoff Λ₂ (let’s call this theory T₂). In this scenario, theory T₁ is said to be connected to theory T₂ via an RG flow (in other words, T₁ flows into T₂). RG flows are irreversible, because you cannot undo coarse-graining without additional information, and thus an EFT with a lower cutoff (called the IR theory) can result from several EFTs with higher cutoffs (called the UV theories). This, in turn, implies that low-energy behaviours of many UV theories will be the same if they flow to the same IR theory. It is this fact that makes it clear that in order to describe the low-energy phenomenon, the details of the small-scale physics is irrelevant, and therefore we can have an effective description at low energies in the form of an EFT. Below, we will discuss three different examples of effective theories to describe the predictive power of such theories.
Fermi Theory of Beta Decay

The elegance of the idea behind EFTs becomes especially clear when examined through concrete historical examples. The first of these is Fermi’s theory of the radioactive decay called the beta decay, which predates the modern language of EFT but perfectly exemplifies the logic behind it. Since the early twentieth century, physicists were well acquainted with the fact that when nuclei undergo a beta decay, they produce an electron and a daughter nucleus, but the mechanism behind this decay lacked an explanation. This was the case because the interaction responsible for this decay (which is called the weak interaction) was not understood at that time. In addition, the electron was emitted at varying energies, which led Wolfgang Pauli to hypothesise an additional particle in the decay products, the antineutrino. However, the distribution of electrons at different energies, shown in Figure 1, still required an explanation. In the 1930s, Enrico Fermi sought to explain the mechanism by proposing a point-like four-particle interaction between a neutron, proton, electron, and antineutrino, described by a single constant that quantifies the strength of the force (such constants are called coupling constants) called the Fermi constant G_F. The theory made accurate predictions for nuclear beta decay rates, despite the fact that Fermi did not understand the underlying weak interaction. His theory violated special relativity at sufficiently high energies and broke down completely at energies much larger than the nuclear scale. But within its domain—below the energy scale of nuclear reactions (called the MeV-scale)—it worked extremely well.

From the modern perspective, Fermi theory is an effective field theory with a cutoff around the mass of the W boson (M_W ∼ 80GeV). At energies far below M_W, the W boson is too heavy to appear as a real particle in the process, so we can “integrate it out”. In practice, this means we do not treat the W field as an active degree of freedom at low energies. Instead, its effects show up indirectly as an effective contact interaction among the lighter fields. The consequence is a local four-particle operator suppressed by 1/M_(W)², which is precisely Fermi’s G_F. This theory cannot make sense for arbitrarily high energy scales because it would give infinite answers at sufficiently high energies, and those infinities cannot be cured. Such a theory is called a non-renormalisable theory, meaning it cannot be extended to arbitrarily high energies without introducing new physics. The nonrenormalisable nature of the Fermi theory is not a flaw, but a mark of its effectiveness. The breakdown of the theory at high energy is not a conceptual failure but a diagnostic. It tells us roughly the energy scale where new physics must appear. Fermi’s theory was not “wrong”; it was the correct low-energy description of the weak interaction.

The Fermi theory example also makes clear what is meant by the hierarchy of descriptions in an EFT. In the low-energy description, physics is described very well by the Fermi theory, which results from the form of a mathematical object called an operator. Physics at higher energies involves contributions from other forms of operators (called the higher-order operators). The contributions from these higher-order operators do not matter much at low energies because these contributions are suppressed by powers of E/M_W, where E is the energy of the process. Therefore, at small energies, these contributions are small, and you do not need the full Standard Model to compute beta decay to high precision. The low-energy world is predictable using the EFT precisely because the effects from high-energy physics are negligible at low energies.
Rayleigh Scattering

A second classic example illustrating the conceptual power of effective theories is Rayleigh scattering—the mechanism behind the blue colour of the sky. Rayleigh scattering describes how light interacts with particles much smaller than its wavelength. Lord Rayleigh found in the nineteenth century that the probability of scattering scales like 1/λ⁴, where λ is the wavelength of the scattering light. It explains why shorter (bluer) wavelengths scatter more strongly, giving us the blue colour of the sky. However, Rayleigh did not know about the atomic or molecular structure underpinning this effect.

From a modern standpoint, Rayleigh scattering is another effective theory. For wavelengths much longer than atomic sizes, one can approximate the atom as a point particle which can attain a property called the dipole moment. The dipole moment of a charge distribution is a measure of how far positive and negative charges are in this distribution. This changes when it is put in some external electrical field, and the standard theory of electromagnetism shows that when the dipole moment of a charge distribution changes with time, this distribution emits electromagnetic radiation of its own.

During Rayleigh scattering, the electric field of incoming light causes the dipole moment of the atom to change with time, and the fluctuating dipole radiates light (which is called scattered light, since it is released as the result of some incoming light). One does not need to compute the complicated electronic structure of the atom at these wavelengths. All one needs is the coarse-grained property—the dipole moment. Finer atomic details contribute only corrections proportional to the powers of a/λ, where a is the atomic size. This ratio is small for the regime where the wavelength of the scattered light is large as compared to the atomic size. Long-wavelength light is incapable of probing short-distance structure, so the atom appears structureless. The EFT of Rayleigh scattering succeeds because the world has this hierarchical structure. If light wavelengths were comparable to atomic sizes in everyday life, the sky would not be blue; it would be a chaotic mess reflecting the microscopic structure of air molecules. But the vast separation of scales ensures a cleanly predictable phenomenon.

Taken together, these examples point towards a unifying theme—when there is a large separation of scales between the physics you probe and the microscopic details, the world becomes simple. The microscopic theory “flows” into a coarse-grained theory with fewer parameters and more universal behaviour. Effective theories provide the bridge between these levels of description.
General Relativity as an EFT

The perspective of EFTs has profound implications for how we understand even our most celebrated fundamental theories. Nowhere is this clearer than in the application of EFT methods to general relativity, a programme heavily advocated by people like Steven Weinberg and put into shape by John Donoghue[1] in the 1990s and developed further in his later work.[2] Fully quantum mechanical GR is known to be pathological, as attempts to quantise GR using the techniques of QFT run into divergences that cannot be suppressed (non-renormalisable).[3] This suggests that GR is incompatible with quantum mechanics for predictions at arbitrarily high energies (e.g., predictions for the beginning of our universe) unless it is replaced entirely by a new, more fundamental theory such as string theory, loop quantum gravity, or something else.

However, we can certainly view GR as an EFT, valid at energies far below the Planck scale. From this perspective, the fact that GR is non-renormalisable is not a sign of failure. It is exactly what you expect from an effective description. It is analogous to Fermi’s theory or the EFT of Rayleigh scattering. At low energies, one does not need the full quantum theory of gravity. The leading terms in the Einstein–Hilbert action (the action which gives us the Einstein field equations), plus a hierarchy of higher-order terms suppressed by powers of the Planck scale[4] suffice. Quantum fluctuations of the gravitational field produce calculable, universal corrections to gravitational interactions. These corrections are suppressed by powers of E/M_(Pl), making them utterly negligible at accessible energies. But their calculability establishes that gravity is a perfectly consistent quantum mechanical effective field theory.

In his landmark paper, Donoghue demonstrated that, by treating GR as an EFT, one can compute quantum corrections to Newton’s gravitational potential (which itself results in the low-energy limit of GR). The result shows that Newton’s 1/r potential receives tiny, universal corrections scaling like 1/r³ and suppressed by Gh/c³. These corrections do not depend on the details of whatever more fundamental theory completes gravity at very high energies. They arise purely from low-energy physics such as that of the universal quantum fluctuations of the massless graviton. This is the hallmark of an effective field theory—predictions at low energies do not depend on the unknown high-energy theory. GR treated as an EFT makes genuine quantum mechanical predictions independent of quantum gravity’s deeper structure.

Fermi’s four-particle interaction is not wrong. Instead, it is the correct description of weak interactions in the MeV regime. Rayleigh’s 1/λ⁴ scattering law is not a lucky approximation; it is the universal low-energy limit of light interacting with matter. Donoghue’s EFT of gravity is not a provisional workaround; it is the correct quantum description of gravity at accessible energies. These theories are windows to the modal structure of the world, where it manifests at the relevant scales. They remain indispensable, not despite their non-fundamental nature, but because of it. EFTs, therefore, stand not as temporary fixes but as one of the deepest insights into how physical theories relate across scales. It reframes the question of what it means for a theory to be true, replacing the simplistic “fundamental or false” dichotomy with a richer, more realistic picture: theories are true in the regimes where the patterns they describe dominate. This understanding allows us to appreciate the conceptual beauty that arises when we stop forcing theories into boxes they were never meant to occupy.
Effective Realism

Scientific realism is the position that the universe described by science is a real, mind-independent world, and our best scientific theories are approximately true descriptions of it. In recent years, a growing number of philosophers have argued that the traditional way of thinking about scientific realism is ill-suited to the actual structure of modern physics. The usual realist picture treats theories as if they aspire to be literal, all-scale descriptions of the world’s fundamental constituents and interprets them in isolation from other theories. This view assumes that a good scientific theory must be interpretable as a fully true description of Nature, from the smallest scales to the largest. However, quantum mechanics, quantum field theory, and even everyday classical physics resist such a reading. Instead, they present a patchwork of models, approximations, and scale-dependent behaviours. The idea that a scientific realist must take any one of these as a complete, fundamental ontology has become increasingly implausible. From this landscape, effective realism has emerged as an alternative.

Effective realism (ER) starts from a simple fact: even our most successful theories are effective, meaning that they work within restricted domains. It asks us to be realists only about those parts of a theory that actually play a role in explaining and predicting phenomena at the energy scale where the theory is valid. Unlike the traditional realist view, ER does not require a theory to be true in every respect, or to have a unique, global ontology. Instead, it focuses on what a theory gets right where it is meant to apply. As discussed earlier, the structure of EFTs shows that physical phenomena depend only weakly on the fine details of physics at much shorter distances, and physics at one scale can often be understood independently of what happens at more fundamental scales. What matters for realism is robustness: the parts of a theory that survive changes in cutoff, formulation, and modelling choices.

As an example, this shift in emphasis provides a principled way of dealing with the fact that empirical results are not enough to uniquely determine the correct interpretation of quantum mechanics. The various interpretations like Everettian, Bohmian, and informationtheoretic disagree profoundly about ontology yet reproduce all the same empirical results. The effective realist response is to note that despite their metaphysical disagreements, they share large amounts of structure, such as those of the evolution of a quantum mechanical system and the patterns arising from decoherence. These shared structures, which all interpretations must reproduce to be empirically adequate, are robust in precisely the sense that effective realism cares about. Focusing realist commitments on this common structural core bypasses interpretive stalemates without giving up realism.

A similar story unfolds in quantum field theory. The theories used in particle physics are not defined at arbitrarily small scales and, in many cases, cannot even be given mathematically rigorous definitions at all scales. They depend on regulators, cutoffs, renormalisation schemes, and approximations that explicitly encode their limited domains of applicability. Yet physicists extract precise, reliable predictions from them by focusing on cutoff-invariant or regulatorinsensitive quantities. In other words, the reliability of QFT emerges from the separation of scales, not from any claim to fundamental, allscale truth. ER captures this successfully because it is realist about those degrees of freedom and structures that remain after the artefacts of regularisation are washed away.

This is where ontic structural realism (OSR) becomes essential. OSR provides the metaphysical resources ER needs in order to count as a genuine form of realism, rather than as a cautious form of empiricism. Instead of treating objects as metaphysically primitive, OSR treats structure, in particular modal structure, as ontologically fundamental. It says that the entities that are real are the stable patterns, the lawful relationships, the constraints on possibility, and the mathematical structures that encode them. Objects or entities emerge from the roles they play within these structures, not from their intrinsic natures or properties.

Under this view, the shared structures across the interpretations of quantum mechanics such as decoherence, and the modal organisation of states, are not mere mathematical conveniences. They are themselves part of the world’s modal structure. Similarly, the cutoff-invariant features of QFT are not artefacts of approximation but reflect the genuine organisation of Nature across scales. Even the explanatory structures of superseded theories, like Newtonian gravity, can be retained without inconsistency, because OSR interprets them as scale-bound patterns rather than as literal, fundamental descriptions. Newtonian forces and relativistic curvature are both real but at different scales and in different regimes.

A key advantage of OSR is that it provides a principled way to talk about what the philosopher Daniel Dennett called real patterns. Borrowing from the work of Dennett, and expanded on by Ladyman and Ross, a real pattern is one that is stable, information rich, and detectable across multiple perspectives or models. Quarks, hadrons, phonons, vortices, classical trajectories, and even biological or economic structures can qualify as real patterns when they exhibit this kind of robustness. Effective realism points to robustness as a good guide to what we should take seriously, but without OSR it lacks a metaphysics explaining why robustness tracks reality. OSR fills this gap by treating these stable patterns and constraints as part of the world’s structure, not just features of our descriptions.

What emerges from the combination of effective realism and OSR is a new form of scientific realism that is aligned with the actual practice of physics. Instead of demanding a single, all-purpose ontology, it recognises that what exists depends on scale, that physical theories describe layers of structure, and that these layers are unified not by objects but by patterns and modal relationships. This unified framework has implications for several longstanding philosophical debates. As discussed earlier, it reframes the interpretation problem in quantum mechanics by grounding realism in shared structural commitments rather than in a specific ontology, resolves worries about the mathematical and conceptual status of quantum field theories by focusing on cutoff-invariant features, and clarifies how superseded theories can retain partial ontological validity. Better yet, it does all this without collapsing into anti-realism or instrumentalism, because OSR ensures that the structures to which we commit ourselves are taken as genuine parts of the world.
Newtonian and Einsteinian Physics

An immediate application of the ideas originating from ER that comes to mind is to understand the relationship between Newtonian and Einsteinian physics. It is common in popular accounts of physics to frame the arrival of special relativity and general relativity as a dramatic overthrow of the Newtonian worldview. According to this narrative, Newtonian mechanics and Newtonian gravity dominated scientific thinking for two centuries until Einstein revealed them to be fundamentally mistaken by declaring that space is not absolute, time is not universal, gravity is not a force, and all the intuitive notions of the Newtonian picture evaporate in the face of a deeper, more accurate understanding.

This “Einstein disproves Newton” story is rhetorically satisfying, but it is philosophically shallow and physically misleading. It treats scientific theories as if they live or die according to whether they mirror fundamental ontology, and it assumes that successor theories replace their predecessors wholesale. That picture is untenable given what we now know about effective theories, scale separation, and the structural relationships between different physical descriptions.

If one accepts the premise that “a theory which is only true in a particular regime cannot be a true description of Nature and thus comes with no ontological baggage” then even our best theories today—GR and the Standard Model of particle physics—can be argued to have no ontological baggage. We do know that GR does not give sensible predictions for very strong gravitational fields—GR predicts that singularities are inevitable under gravitational collapse, and when GR is paired up with QFT, it gives infinite probabilities for particle scattering under the gravitational interaction. Moreover, the concept of a field (and spacetime itself, where the fields live) may break down at very high energies. Following the previously mentioned premise would then render spacetime, its curvature, and the fields that live on it to be non-ontological, despite the fact that all these entities are excellent tools to describe physics at the scales that we encounter.

For the Newtonian and Einsteinian regimes, a more accurate premise and one consistent with the conceptual lessons extracted from effective realism and ontic structural realism, is that Newtonian mechanics and Newtonian gravity are neither false nor obsolete. Rather, they are spectacularly successful effective theories and approximations that capture real, modal features of the world at the scales where they were meant to apply. Far from being destroyed by relativity, Newtonian physics survives inside relativistic physics as a limiting structure, retaining explanatory and predictive power across vast domains of the natural world. The lens of ER shows that Newtonian physics was never meant to be fundamental, and that relativity does not invalidate the reality of the structures it described.

The modern concept of an effective theory allows us to see this clearly. In physics, a theory is effective when its success depends on the separation of scales—situations where certain variables vary slowly, certain forces dominate, or certain velocities remain much smaller than others. In these regimes, a simpler theory can describe the system accurately because the details of the deeper, faster, or smaller-scale dynamics become irrelevant.

Newtonian mechanics is exactly of this kind. It describes systems whose velocities are small compared to the speed of light, whose energies are too low to require relativistic effects, and whose gravitational fields are sufficiently weak that the curvature of spacetime is negligible. Under these conditions—the conditions of planets, falling apples, projectiles, engineering structures, biological organisms, vehicles, rocks, rivers, and practically every macroscopic system we encounter—the Newtonian description forms a well-defined limit of the deeper relativistic theory. That is, there is a parameter regime in which Newtonian equations emerge from relativistic ones. When velocities are much smaller than the speed of light (denoted as c), the Lorentz transformations converge toward the Galilean transformations. When gravitational potentials are weak and vary slowly across space, the Einstein field equations reduce to the equation that describes Newtonian gravity (i.e., Poisson’s equation), and the geodesic equation reduces to the equation of motion of a particle which results from Newton’s law of gravitation. The Newtonian limit is not a mistake or an illusion. It is the regime where the modal structure encoded in general relativity simplifies into a pattern that Newton’s laws capture with extraordinary fidelity.

Under effective realism, this means Newtonian mechanics is true in its domain—not just useful, not just approximately valid, but tracking genuine structural features of the world. It captures invariant relationships between mass, force, acceleration, energy, and momentum that remain robust across the entire range where the theory is effective. These patterns reappear under multiple derivations: in classical mechanics, Hamiltonian formulations, symplectic geometry, and the low-velocity limits of relativistic dynamics. In the language of real patterns, Newtonian physics identifies modal structures that remain detectable and predictive across numerous independent methods of modelling. That robustness is the hallmark of ontological significance. Even if the Newtonian view does not extend to all scales, the patterns it reveals are real at the scale at which they arise.

The apparent conceptual contradictions between Newtonian and relativistic physics—absolute time vs. relativity of simultaneity, and forces vs. curvature—do not demonstrate that Newton was wrong. They demonstrate that Newton described a pattern that emerges after coarse-graining. Consider the case of time. In Newton’s theory, time is absolute because two observers agree on the simultaneity of distant events. In relativity, simultaneity becomes frame-dependent. Yet the Newtonian conception of time remains an excellent approximation whenever relative velocities are negligible. The relativity of simultaneity is not falsified by Newton’s picture. Instead, it is invisible within the scale regime where Newton’s picture is effective. OSR teaches us to avoid conflating differences in structural regime with inconsistency. Just as we do not call hydrodynamics “wrong” because it breaks down at molecular scales, nor do we call classical thermodynamics “false” because statistical mechanics reveals deeper microstructure, the structural differences between Newtonian time and relativistic spacetime do not mark one as true and the other as false. They mark different levels of structural description.

The same applies to gravity. If one insists that Newtonian gravity must be literally interpreted as a universal force acting instantaneously at a distance, then relativity certainly makes that picture untenable. However, Newton himself took the action-at-a-distance problem as a mystery, not as a dogma. Moreover, within the domain of validity, Newtonian gravity captures a real structural feature: massive bodies attract each other in a way that produces orbits, free fall, tides, and planetary motion. From the structural realist perspective, these are not illusions. They correspond to modal patterns that survive across multiple theoretical views. GR replaces the force with curvature, but the patterns of elliptical orbits, falling bodies, conservation of energy and angular momentum remain. The mechanism, and the ontology at the fundamental scale change, but the pattern is preserved, and it is this preservation that gives Newtonian gravity its durable reality.

The most important point is that relativity does not revise the world in Newton’s domain, but the world outside it. The transition from Newtonian to relativistic physics was not a discovery that Newton’s world never existed, but a discovery that Newton’s world is part of a larger, hierarchical structure of physical description. Modern physics suggests that there may not be a single theory that gives the correct ontology at all scales. Instead, there may be a nesting of effective theories, each with its own real patterns, its own modal structures, and its own domain. Newtonian mechanics is one such layer, which is astonishingly accurate, conceptually illuminating, and ontologically meaningful at the human scale.

We do acknowledge that this suggestion from modern physics can be misleading. Even if modern physics seems to suggest that there may not be a single theory that gives the correct ontology at all scales, it does not mean that there cannot be a theory that can achieve it. Ideas like string theory are efforts to achieve precisely this. It may also turn out that descriptions at different scales are related to each other by some dualities. We should not be surprised by the presence of such dualities, as we have seen such dualities in the past, e.g., the Kramers–Wannier duality that relates the highand low-temperature behaviours of an idealised magnet.

The lesson to draw, then, is not that relativity shows Newton was wrong, but that Newton was right within the realm where Nature manifests the patterns he described. His theories are not false theories waiting to be replaced by truer ones, but they are effective theories whose reality is guaranteed by their scale-robustness and modal stability. The apparent supersession is not a replacement of truth by truth, but a refinement of modal structure at a smaller scale.

In this sense, Newtonian mechanics and gravity remain as real today as they were in late seventeenth century. They continue to reveal genuine structural relationships in the world, i.e., relationships that both special and general relativity preserve in the appropriate limit. To declare them false because they do not apply at relativistic scales is to misunderstand the very logic of scientific theories and the nature of physical ontology. A theory can be non-fundamental yet still be true in its domain. A worldview can be incomplete yet still correctly describe the slice of reality for which it was formulated. And scientific progress, when properly understood, is not the destruction of old worlds by new ones, but the integration of multiple layers of real structure into a deeper, more nuanced picture of Nature.
Conclusion

Taken together, effective field theory, effective realism, and OSR offer a unified picture of how scientific theories relate across scales without forcing a false choice between truth and fundamentality. The central lesson is that progress in physics is rarely a story of radical rupture. Instead, it is a story of continuity in structure across changing descriptions. OSR provides the metaphysical explanation for this continuity by proposing that what survives the process of theory change are not particular objects or fundamental ontologies, but robust modal structures, which include patterns of dependence, constraint, and possibility that remain persistent across regimes.

From this perspective, the emergence of a deeper theory does not undermine the reality of its predecessors. Rather, it explains why they worked. This point is especially clear in contemporary discussions of quantum gravity. Any viable theory of QG should reproduce the behaviour of gravity that we see at low energies. OSR is a stronger statement, because in addition to the requirement that we just mentioned, OSR also says that some kind of structure from the known theory of gravity should be preserved in a quantum theory of gravity. For example, if a quantum theory of gravity declares spacetime as non-fundamental, then there should be some entity in this theory which replaces spacetime, and the relationships of this entity with other entities should be the same as the relationship that spacetime has with the counterparts of these other entities in the known theory of gravity. This is what the preservation of structure means.

As an example, string theory is often portrayed as a dramatic break from both quantum field theory and general relativity. Yet its most striking feature is precisely the opposite. In appropriate limits, it reproduces effective quantum field theories, classical spacetime, and Einstein’s equations. The counterpart of particles in string theory are tiny strings, which behave like particles at low energies. To show that string theory actually describes our world, one needs to show that it does entail the Standard Model of particle physics. This is a matter of ongoing research. OSR proposes exactly this behaviour: new theories refine, extend, and reorganise existing structures instead of abolishing them. Therefore, the principles that are set up by OSR can be used to reduce the number of possible theories when we are trying to find the deeper theories. We should only entertain those candidate theories that have some structure (with the right relationships) that can be seen as reminiscent of the structure in the known theory of reality. Otherwise, it is hard, if not impossible, to get the known theory as a limiting procedure of the deeper theory.

Seen through the lens of effective realism and OSR, modern physics supports a realism that is pluralistic but not fragmented, scale-relative but not anti-realist. Effective realism, grounded by OSR, captures the fact that science actually advances by revealing a hierarchy of real structures, where each structure is genuine in its own domain, and where they collectively form a coherent picture of the physical world.
